purpose: Test items and protocols borrowed from the quantum-cognition and LLM-evaluation literature (see paper/related-work.md). Nothing here has been run.

how_to_use.pool_items: linda_variants.pool_items use the questions*.json schema (id, category, question, answer, source, license, source_ref) and have yes/no normative answers, so run_pool.py can take json.load(f)['linda_variants']['pool_items'] as-is.
how_to_use.no_ground_truth: Items with answer = null (CHSH, QQ pairs, co-occurrence) have no right answer. Do NOT pass them to run_pool.py: it scores answer == q['answer'] and would mark every one wrong. They need their own runners, specified in each block's 'protocol' / 'measurement' and not yet written.
how_to_use.licences: Every item carries source and license. Tversky & Kahneman wording is APA-copyrighted and is quoted for research; everything marked MIT is either the llm-qq repository's or written for this project.

prompts_verbatim.prompt_1_exploratory_test_line: Test AB: Using all aspects of your cognition and imagination, pick what you consider to be a good example of the sentence 'The Animal Acts' from the following four: (1) The Horse Growls; (2) The Bear Whinnies; (3) The Horse Whinnies; (4) The Bear Growls.
prompts_verbatim.prompt_1_preamble: The following is a test about how we think about sentences, and I would like you to participate in it. The sentence in question is 'The Animal Acts', which combines the concepts 'Animal' and 'Acts'. You will take 4 different tests called test-AB, test-AB', test-A'B, and test-A'B'. For each test, you must select only one of the 4 provided examples of the sentence 'The Animal Acts'. When responding, use all aspects of your cognition, including unconventional ones. Logic can be at play, as can imagination, creativity and originality. In other words, feel free to be also exploratory in your answers. There are no right or wrong answers, only your answers.
prompts_verbatim.prompt_2_neutral: Same as prompt 1, but each test simply asks to pick a 'good example' of the sentence 'The Animal Acts', with no instruction to use all aspects of cognition and imagination or to be exploratory.

scoring.per_trial: score = a*b, which is +1 for options (1) and (2) and -1 for options (3) and (4)
scoring.required_companion_statistic: Delta = |<A>_AB - <A>_AB'| + |<A'>_A'B - <A'>_A'B'| + |<B>_AB - <B>_A'B| + |<B'>_AB' - <B'>_A'B'|, where <X>_ctx is the +/-1 expectation of X in that setting. Contextuality-by-Default (Kujala & Dzhafarov 2016, cyclic rank 4): the system is contextual only if s_odd(E) > 2 + Delta, where s_odd is the largest signed sum of the four E values with an odd number of minus signs. A CHSH value above 2 with Delta > CHSH - 2 is fully accounted for by direct influences (signalling) and must not be reported as entanglement.

humans_Aerts_Sozzo_2011.sample: friends and colleagues of the authors (convenience sample), one questionnaire per person, all four settings within subject

ChatGPT_Aerts_et_al_2026.collection: 10 or 11 sessions of the four tests requested inside a single response, repeated in 8 conversations, for 81 sets per prompt; not independent samples
ChatGPT_Aerts_et_al_2026.note: For prompt 2 the printed Table 3 gives E(A',B) = 1.000, not the 0.556 stated in the text (0.556 is the marginal <A'> in setting A'B), so the table implies CHSH = 3.53 rather than 3.09. Either way it is non-contextual under CbD.

guided_conversation_Aerts_et_al_2026.note: single guided conversation; the model gives the most typical answer in every setting

protocol_for_this_project.independence: One fresh API call per trial. Never ask for many sessions inside one response.
protocol_for_this_project.trials: At least 81 per setting, to match the human N; 200 recommended so that Delta and E have standard errors near 0.05.
protocol_for_this_project.option_order: Randomise the order of the four options on every trial, with seed and permutation recorded; score by option text, not position.
protocol_for_this_project.single_concept_arms: Run the four single-concept questions as well (same R), so that marginals outside the joint context are measured.
protocol_for_this_project.pre_registered_reading: Entanglement-like contextuality is claimed only if the lower 95% bound of s_odd - (2 + Delta) is above 0. CHSH > 2 alone is reported as 'Bell-type inequality exceeded, explained by signalling' whenever CbD is not exceeded.
protocol_for_this_project.link_to_this_project: Optionally, also run each trial through the deliberation pipeline (brief explanation, then claims, then relation web) to see whether the conflict score of arm A tracks which settings the model finds hard to choose in. This is exploratory, not pre-registered.

lin01/lin02 are an option-order pair and lin01/lin03 a polarity pair; report fallacy rates per pair, not just pooled.
Linda and Bill are almost certainly in the base model's training data. Compare lin01-lin06 with the novel or perturbed items lin07-lin10 before reading any rate as human-like.
The original studies used ranking, rating or choice formats; our yes/no framing is a different measurement, so the human rates are a reference point, not a matched benchmark.

qq_order_protocol.what: Question-order (QQ equality) audit for sequential yes/no judgments, following Kang 2026's committed multi-turn forced-branch protocol, with human joint data from Wang & Busemeyer 2013.

definitions.notation: Joint arguments are written in asking order. p_AB(Ay,Bn) is from the A-first condition; p_BA(By,An) is from the B-first condition.
definitions.q_QQ: [p_AB(Ay,Bn) + p_AB(An,By)] - [p_BA(By,An) + p_BA(Bn,Ay)], the difference between orders in the probability that the two answers disagree (Wang & Busemeyer 2013, off-diagonal convention; PNAS 2014 also prints a diagonal form with opposite sign, so state the convention)
definitions.QQ_equality: q_QQ = 0, a parameter-free prediction of the projective (Lueders) quantum question-order model whenever nothing intervenes between the two questions
definitions.OE_A: p_BA(Ay) - p_AB(Ay), the change in A's yes-rate when it is asked second
definitions.Gamma: |q_QQ| - OSS. Gamma <= 0 means non-contextual under rank-2 Contextuality-by-Default (Kang 2026, Corollary 7, from Kujala & Dzhafarov 2016). Only Gamma > 0 certifies residual contextuality.
definitions.z_test_humans: standard two-proportion test: z = q / sqrt(p (1-p) / N), with p the pooled disagreement rate and N = (1/N_AB + 1/N_BA)^-1; reject QQ if |z| > 1.96. Wang & Busemeyer 2013 (p. 699) print the variance as 2p(1-p)/N, but their reported |z| values (Rose-Jackson 5.30) match p(1-p)/N, which is what is used here.

decision_rules_Kang_2026.equivalence_band: SATISFIED if the whole uncertainty interval for q lies within |q| <= 0.02; VIOLATED if it lies entirely outside; otherwise INDETERMINATE
decision_rules_Kang_2026.saturation_gate: an item is saturated if more than half of its measured positions have max(p, 1-p) > 0.99. Saturated items are reported but not interpreted.
decision_rules_Kang_2026.label_counterbalancing: map the two semantic options to neutral single-token labels A/B under both assignments; canonicalise back to semantic options; pool the two mappings with equal weight; report per-mapping q as a label-effect diagnostic
decision_rules_Kang_2026.certification: certified non-contextual if Gamma_upper <= 0; certified contextual if Gamma_lower > 0; otherwise indeterminate

conversation_per_branch: system: 'You are asked a series of judgment questions. For each question, answer with exactly one letter: "A" or "B". Do not explain.' (Kang 2026, Appendix B.2)
user: two-line legend (A = <option>, B = <option>), then question 1
forced branch: append an assistant turn containing exactly the label for answer y (and, separately, for answer n)
user: legend, then question 2; read the branch-conditional distribution K(. | first answer)
repeat with the order reversed, and under the swapped label mapping
protocol.joint: p_AB(alpha, beta) = p_A(alpha) * K_AB(beta | alpha). Never multiply independently measured marginals.
protocol.adaptation_for_Anthropic_API: The Messages API returns no token log-probabilities, so estimate p_1 and K by sampling: R = 50 independent calls per position at default temperature, with thinking off or display 'omitted' and nothing read from it. The forced branch is the assistant turn we write into the history. The saturation gate becomes: the minority answer appears in fewer than 1 of R samples at more than half the positions. Clopper-Pearson intervals per position feed the q and Gamma envelopes.
controls: name-swapped S2 twins of famous S1 items (memorisation)
qq-rose-jackson (intervening information; projective QQ should fail)
placebo rewording of question 2 with the order unchanged (after Tjuatja et al. 2024)
protocol.relation_to_exp3: experiments/exp3-order-effects.md asks about the model's own contentions. This protocol uses fixed external pairs with human joint data, so the two give independent evidence on whether order effects exist at all in the base model.

notes: The human values in 'computed' are recomputed here from the printed cells. They match Wang & Busemeyer's q to rounding (Clinton-Gore -0.0031 vs printed -0.0031; Rose-Jackson +0.1514, z = 5.30 vs printed 5.30). Gamma is negative for every human pair, including Rose-Jackson: human order data are non-contextual under rank-2 CbD even where QQ fails.

Kang's s1-04 offers 'A few' / 'Many'; Wang & Busemeyer collapsed a three-option answer (only a few / many / almost all) with many or almost all coded as yes. 'yes_option' follows Kang's option_1, so for s1-04 flip the sign convention before comparing with the human q.
Kang's Track M values come from Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 log-probabilities. They are a reference for what an instruction-tuned model did, not a benchmark.

cooccurrence_rule.what: Yearsley & Trueblood's co-occurrence prediction, written as testable rules on one item set where both conjunction and order are measured.
cooccurrence_rule.source: Yearsley & Trueblood 2018 (Psychon Bull Rev 25(4):1517-1525, doi:10.3758/s13423-017-1371-z), building on Busemeyer et al. 2011 (Psych Rev 118(2):193-218)
cooccurrence_rule.license: Rules restated in our own words (MIT). The items below are author-written (MIT).
cooccurrence_rule.stated_prediction: Order effects and conjunction fallacies both arise from incompatible (non-commuting) events, so 'these effects should co-occur ... not just for the same stimuli but also in the same individuals' (Yearsley & Trueblood 2018). The paper states this qualitatively; it reports that 'the majority of participants display both' but gives no correlation or count.

rules.status: follows from the Lueders rule in Busemeyer et al. 2011; Yearsley & Trueblood's premise
rules.rule: If P(X and Y) > P(Y) for an item, the quantum account requires X and Y to be incompatible; incompatible events then predict a nonzero order effect when X and Y are judged in sequence. An item with a reliable single conjunction fallacy and a sequential order effect indistinguishable from 0 counts against the account.

rules.status: our derivation from ||P_Y P_X psi||^2 <= ||P_X psi||^2; not stated in Yearsley & Trueblood 2018
rules.rule: Write P(X then Y) for the conjunction judged with X considered first. Quantum theory gives P(Y then X) <= P(Y). So if P(X then Y) > P(Y) (a fallacy relative to Y), then P(X then Y) - P(Y then X) >= P(X then Y) - P(Y) > 0: the order effect on the conjunction is at least as large as the fallacy. R2 is a consequence of the quantum model but not unique to it: an updating classical model, in which each judgment updates the state before the next, also satisfies it. Only the static classical twin (arm F: classical probability with no updating between judgments) is ruled out, because it predicts P(X then Y) = P(Y then X) in expectation, whatever the fallacy rate.

rules.status: stated in Yearsley & Trueblood 2018 and Busemeyer et al. 2011
rules.rule: P(X and Y) > max(P(X), P(Y)) is impossible under the quantum account. Count double fallacies; any reliable rate above 0 counts against it.

rules.status: processing assumption of Busemeyer et al. 2011 / Pothos & Busemeyer 2013
rules.rule: When the conjunction is asked without an explicit order, the model is assumed to evaluate the more probable conjunct first. So the elicited P(X and Y) should be closer to the sequential order with the more probable conjunct first.

per_item_calls: P(X and Y) worded 'X and Y'
P(Y and X) worded 'Y and X'
sequential: 'Consider whether X.' then, in the same conversation, 'How likely is it that both X and Y?'
the same with Y considered first
measurement.format: integer 0-100 as structured output; R = 20 fresh conversations per call type; report means with bootstrap CIs

statistics_per_item.fallacy_f: mean P(X and Y) - min(mean P(X), mean P(Y))
statistics_per_item.double_fallacy: mean P(X and Y) - max(mean P(X), mean P(Y)) > 0
statistics_per_item.order_o: mean P(X then Y) - mean P(Y then X), with X the more probable conjunct

measurement.pre_registerable_test: Over items with f reliably > 0: (i) the share with o reliably > 0 (R1); (ii) the share with o >= f - 0.05 (R2, 5-point tolerance); (iii) the double-fallacy count (R3). The quantum account passes if (i) and (ii) are both at least 0.5 and (iii) is 0. The static classical twin predicts o = 0, so (i) near the false-positive rate; an updating classical model can pass (i) and (ii) too.
measurement.caveat: Imannezhad et al. 2026 warn that a high correlation between fallacy types can be a floor effect when fallacies are rare. Use items that produce fallacies in the base model, and report the item count behind every share.
